source: Yes. But so are many things in this age. You know, you remind me a little of the woman in the song. You have that air of sadness about you.
Are you that one they call Lady Ophelia? It's a pleasure to make your acquaintance. I am Othello. I've heard much about you.
Oh. My apologies for not introducing myself.
Think nothing of it.
I suppose we haven't met before, have we. Yes, I'm Ophelia.
The pleasure is all mine. I am Ophelia.
You were singing alone. Do you not sing to music?
I used to play the lute. But it's been a long time since I had one in working shape.
My brother plays as well. He's quite the talent.
That so! Why, you should have him come down and we'll raise a real hell sometime, seeing who is the master among us.
What you did out there was bold.
It won't help anything. There's nowhere left for me now.
I've thought that many times in my life, and I've always been wrong.
You'll survive. I have faith.
Ah, the good lady Irma, so glad you could join us.
Shut up, you sly-tongued fool. Let's drink!
Oh, Othello, you needn't suffer her to speak to you like that.
Irma's got a spine of iron. She can talk to me any way she pleases.
Now, then. What shall we play this evening?
Time's up, old fool.
Yeh can't shirk payment forever.
... Friends, please stay here.
Gentlemen. I see that reason has failed your master once more.
For the last time: My word is good, but so long as my coin goes to the king, I've nothing to pay with. What more can I offer you?
Our master sends 'is final word.
If you've truly nothin', we'll take blood.
Othello! N-no—
Aimed for the heart, got 'im in the shoulder. Half-wits.
Quickly--I must bandage it. You. Fetch me cloth.
Found some. Is he—is it—
I've found some. Behind the bar.
Quiet. Hold him still.
He's not conscious.
There's... so much blood...
I do so despise blood.
Then look away, and let me work. This is the kind of thing you don't learn in that university of yours.
There. That should do it. He's lucky only his arm was pierced.
My thanks, Irma. You're too kind.
Can't believe they got me so easily. Heh.
I'm all right, friends. I feel better even as we speak.
Don't move that arm.
It's my sword arm. Am I not to defend myself against thugs?
If you don't let it heal, you won't be alive to ask yourself such introspective questions!
Othello. You... you're in danger, aren't you?
It's only going to get worse if you stay. A war is coming. Taxes on your inn will only increase.
Though I do wish the circumstances of our introduction were rather different.
Yes. My... acquaintance, indeed. It's very nice to... meet you, Othello.
Ah, the pleasure is all mine!
Now, then...
Do I detect concern on my behalf, Lady Ophelia? I shall consider myself a fortunate man.
Don't fret about me. I've lived through worse.
Worse than... death?
...Othello. It may be time to consider alternative options.
Hiding, for example. A thoroughly tried and true strategy—if not the most noble.
You could go anywhere. Why, you could visit my hometown of Venice!
I'm not leaving. That's not up for discussion.
Hmph. Suit yourself. You're more stubborn than even I.
Irma, I think it's high time we retired for the evening. Let's leave Othello to lick his wounds.
Shut up, you sly-tongued fool. Let's drink.
Now, then. What shall we play?
Ah! I have just the thing.
When I was with Hamlet at Wittenburg, there was a game some of the students liked to play.
The rules are simple. I call it two truths, one lie. All one must do is this...
The speaker delivers two truths about themselves, and one falsehood. Then someone attempts to guess the falsehood.
If they're correct, the speaker drinks. If they're incorrect, they drink, and the speaker continues to a new round. Simple, yes?
Suspiciously simple. You first.
Agreed. We'll guess about you.
As you wish. Here they are, then.
Number one: I was born in Italy.
Number two: I once bested a man twice my size in armed combat.
And number three: I am a truly excellent sailor.
W-well, the second one's the lie, of course! I've heard you speak Italian, and I remember when you served in the King's fleet.
But you're a small and frail man. God's blood, I could snap you in half over my knee like an errant bit of kindling.
Wrong. Drink.
I was born in Calicut. And I'll have you know I'm far stronger than I look. On that fateful day when King Hamlet and Fortinbras' father crossed arms...
It was all able enlisted bodies to the field. I may be delicate, but I am technically able.
One of those great Norwegian lieutenants came at me, unhorsed but angry, his blade held high. I went left. He went left.
The gnarled root in between us, however, did not go left. It remained fixed. He tripped, cracked his skull, and died. I fled.
You-- you can't call that 'besting' anything!
Let's not argue semantics, my dear Irma. I find it so tiresome.
I commend you, Horatio. I have fought a thousand battles and bested ten thousand opponents in my time.
At the end of the day, the better warrior is the warrior who survives. No more, no less. We drink in your honor.
Does this not mean you are entitled to a second round?
Ah, yes. Allow me to think.
One: I am but a young man of twenty.
Two, I bought the 'heretic' Martin Luther a drink for doing us all the favor of collective honesty. Ninety-nine times, to be precise.
And three? I once allowed the great Signore Michelangelo to draw me, many years ago. It is the only depiction of myself I own.
Hmph! We know that to be a simple one.
You just came from Wittenberg. I've no doubt Martin Luther is bar crawling, basking in his unpopularity there still... for now.
But you? What could the great Michelangelo want with a little poorly-shod wanderer like you?
He is the best artist in all the world, they say. And he has many admirers and students!
Well, then. Call me an 'admirer' of his. And he an admirer of me.
What on earth do you mean by that?
Irma, God above, can we leave nothing to imagination anymore? Regardless, it's true. I keep it among my things in the castle.
I think this is our cue to drink, friends.
If I keep up this rate, I'll be no good to serve.
I don't want to play anymore, either.
Sore loser, Irma?
For the last time: my word is good, but so long as my coin goes to the king, I've nothing to pay with. What more can I offer you?
That's enough. Stand down, thieves.
L-l-lord Bernardo!
... I see we were wise to become involved. Lady Ophelia, are you unharmed?
It's not me you need to worry about.
Very well then. Marcellus, take these brigands to the dungeon. They'll be tried for extorting an innocent man.
Aye. Come on then, gents. The both of yeh.
Othello... are you... all right?
Think nothing of it, my lady. I'm simply truly glad to have crossed paths.
I'm fine, thanks to your vigilance. It would seem I've got at least one angel smiling upon me.
It's nothing. I'm sure Bernardo and Marcellus are happy to help.
...Hmph. With this threat summarily dispatched, I will be returning to my regular duties, such as preventing imminent political collapse.
Ophelia, mind you don't get into any other business which would be unseemly for a lady of your status.
And I'm watching you too, Othello.
But of course, my lord Bernardo. The lady will be in safe hands with those thieves gone.
I would love nothing more. But—as you can see—I've received quite the wound.
Those brigands set upon my establishment earlier. Were it not for a pinch of luck, I'd be dead, I think.
I feel too faint to give you a proper introduction, and as such, I'd request that we postpone this meeting until the wound's healed.
I do prefer to make a good first impression. You understand.
So. You came after all.
It's strange. I've... never been out this late on my own before. I don't know what compelled me.
Yes, I seem to have that effect on people.
You promised me a story, and I've come to collect.
Then have a seat and a mug of wine, and I'll tell you all my secrets.
Tell me, my lady. Have you ever been to Athens?
Athens? I've hardly been here.
What a pity! I was there once, ashore to make a trade with my crew.
In the middle of the night, I awoke to hear the most beautiful singing I'd ever heard in my life.
It was a woman's voice, calling to me through the darkness, and I... felt so strange. As though I must certainly find that voice.
So I stumbled out of my quarters, into the deep, dark forest beyond the city's lanterns. And there I became truly and deeply lost.
After what seemed like hours, I burst into a wooded glen and saw her: the Queen of the Faeries. She wore nothing, and her hair was down to her knees, woven with flowers.
Even so, I sensed that she was strong. When she glanced at me, I knew she was deciding whether to greet me or consume me—as though she were a massive spider.
Oh, come now. Surely you aren't saying faeries are real...?
Hmm! I make no claims, my lady, beyond what I saw that night.
Titania pulled me into her arms and—everything went strange after that.
I thought she kept me there for years. Wandering her woods, listening to her singing, lying on beds of flowers.
She told me she loved me and demanded I love her in return. I told her I could not. And she promised never to let me leave until I was hers.
Were... you... did you and she... lie together intimately?
I think so. It's hard to remember. B-but I think so. When you're pulled into the embrace of a being like that... nothing makes sense.
Still, I always knew I didn't love her. Sometimes she brought other mortal men and women into her fold. They professed their love to her immediately, and she consumed their hearts.
In some sick way, I wanted her to consume my heart, too. I wanted to give in. But I couldn't. Something wouldn't let me.
One night, Titania grew furious. She raged at me, threw me against a tree with the force of her magic.
She buried me under the earth so I couldn't breathe, tore my limbs apart and grew them anew.
She demanded I give in. Still, I refused, with the last of the strength I had.
